Mentora — Editorial Direction (Exploration)
Editorial Direction · refinement pass

Someone has already walked this path.

Roughly 70% product, 30% editorial: a marketplace you can scan and trust, carrying an identity built from real portraits, an editorial serif used sparingly, a deep pine green, and one small recurring gesture — a hand‑set mark — for the moments something is actually chosen. Nothing botanical is drawn; the influence lives in color, paper, and light.

Status · round four, density pass

Color, type pairing, the hybrid card composition, portraits-as-primary, and the mark remain settled and untouched. This round went after remaining height in the mentor card without touching a single font size: name and role were sitting in paragraph line-height (1.6) meant for multi-line body copy rather than a one-line heading, which cost several pixels each for no reason; the "Next available" label and its slot chips were on two rows and are now one ("Next Tonight · 9:00 PM Tomorrow · 7:30 PM"); and the CTA button's padding and line-height were trimmed slightly. Same six data points, meaningfully shorter card.

Color

A warm ivory foundation, a deep grounded green for brand and primary action, and one restrained warm accent reserved for the signature mark. Semantic color stays a third hue family entirely, so "confirmed" never reads as "on-brand."

Typography

Serif = identity and important human moments. Sans = navigation, controls, and every piece of marketplace data. In practice that means the serif touches perhaps 5–6 words per screen — a name, a hero line — while everything a customer scans to compare mentors (role, rating, price, availability) is sans, bold where it needs to be found fast. No monospace: numbers use tabular figures in the UI face, which reads calmer and less "technical." Audit fix this pass: the profile's stat tiles (4.9 / 248 / 8 yrs) and the dashboard's stat strip were still set in the serif — both are metadata, not identity, so both moved to sans-bold, matching every other number in the product.

Shape, Spacing & Depth

Softer and quieter than a brutalist system: no heavy borders, no hard offset shadows. Structure comes from generous radius, warm-tinted soft shadows, and whitespace — with just enough hairline definition to keep dense screens (like the dashboard) legible.

Signature characteristics

Two traits, both load-bearing rather than decorative. Refined this round to be more selective and more product-forward — remove them and the product still works; keep them and it starts to feel unmistakably like Mentora.

Signature 01 · refined

The mark

Shorter, thicker and drawn from the centre outward rather than left-to-right — a smaller, more deliberate gesture than round one. It now appears in exactly four places: a selected offering, a picked time slot, a confirmed booking, and which profile tab is open. It no longer lives on navigation, hover states, or any CTA, so it still means something when it shows up.

Signature 02 · revised

The hybrid mentor card

Round one's card read as a magazine credit first and a comparison tool second. This round keeps the one editorial cue that earns its place — the serif name — and moves everything else onto tight, aligned sans rows so six mentors compare as easily as any marketplace listing. The portrait still leads and the serif name still carries identity, but rating, price and availability sit on tight aligned rows, and a real button replaces the text link. Compares like a product; still feels like Mentora.

Density, round three: the chosen card was still taller than a marketplace card needs to be. The portrait dropped from a 4:5 crop to 1:1 — still dominant, no longer the majority of the card's height — and the internal rhythm (the rule, the "next available" label, the padding above the button) was tightened throughout. No type sizes changed; the height came out of spacing and the photo, not the words.

Density, round four: line-height was the last hidden cost. One-line elements (the name, the role, the price row) were inheriting body copy's 1.6 line-height; tightened to 1.15–1.3 with zero change to font size. The availability label and its chips merged onto a single row. See the live card on Discover for the current result.

Availability slot states

Selection is communicated through three cues at once — border weight, text color, and the mark — so it never depends on color alone.

Photography

The mentor's face is the primary image everywhere — on Discover, on the profile, and anywhere a booking decision is being made. A light warm grade (a touch of sepia and saturation, not grayscale) unifies portraits without flattening them. Environmental or editorial photography is a rare, secondary device, never a replacement for the person.

Supporting environmental photography (a desk, a window, quiet light) may appear occasionally on the profile page as background context — never in place of the mentor's own portrait, and never on Discover.
